content:
The Olympic Games are considered the world's leading sports event. More than 200 teams from sovereign states and territories participate. The first written records of the Olympics date back to 776 BCE. However, scholars believe the Games were going on long before anyone wrote about them. According to legend, Heracles (Hercules), the half-mortal son of Zeus, founded the Games. The myth explains that after he finished his 12 labors, he built the Olympic Stadium to honor Zeus. The event was named after its location in southern Greece: Olympia. The Olympics were religious and athletic festivals held at the temple of Zeus. Alongside the Games were rituals and sacrifices to honor Zeus and Pelops, Olympia’s hero and mythical king. The Games, held every four years, were so influential that ancient historians began to measure time in four-year increments called olympiads. Each olympiad started on the first or second full moon after the summer solstice.

The Olympic Games reached the height of their success in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE. They gradually declined in importance as the Romans gained power and influence in Greece. While it is uncertain when the Games ended, the most commonly held date is 393 CE. The emperor Theodosius I decreed that all pagan cults and practices be eliminated. The revival of the Olympics began in the 19th century with the Greek War of Independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1821. Many recreations of the event took place in various locations. In 1890, Baron Pierre de Coubertin founded the International Olympic Committee (IOC), intending to establish internationally rotating Olympic Games. The first Games under the IOC were hosted in Athens in 1896. The 1896 Games had 241 participants representing 14 nations. The Olympics are held in different cities around the world. The second Games was in Paris, and the third was held in St. Louis.

Initially, only freeborn male Greeks could participate in the Games. There were no women’s events, and married women weren’t allowed to attend. Some of the first events in the Olympics were the chariot race, foot races, wrestling, equestrian (horse) events, and the pentathlon. The ancient pentathlon had five events: the long jump, discus and javelin throws, a foot race, and wrestling. The modern pentathlon includes fencing, swimming, horse riding, pistol shooting, and running. These events mimic military skills. The ancient games had an event called “pankration,” which means ‘all force.’ It was an early form of mixed martial arts in which athletes combined wrestling and boxing skills. Everything was allowed except biting, gouging, and attacking the genitals. In extreme cases, a pankration bout could even result in the death of one of the opponents. Today, rules and safety measures are overseen by the International Olympic Committee.

The Olympic Games have evolved and grown since ancient Greece. In 2020, more than 14,000 athletes competed in 40 different sports and 448 events. Gymnastics, swimming, track and field, basketball, and weightlifting are some of the most popular events. The Winter Olympics was created to feature snow and ice sports that could not be held during the Summer Games. The first Winter Games was held in Chamonix, France, in 1924. The Winter Games happen every four years and two years after the Summer Games. In 1948, Sir Ludwig Guttmann organized a multi-sport event between many hospitals to coincide with the London Olympics. He wanted to promote the rehabilitation of soldiers after World War II through sport. In 1960, Guttmann brought 400 athletes to Rome to compete in the "Parallel Olympics," which ran parallel with the Summer Olympics. The event, now known as the Paralympics, is a series of international contests for athletes with disabilities.
